name_en: Birthplace of the Tobidashi Bōya (Pop-Out Boy Traffic Signs)
summary_en: The flat, brightly colored silhouette of a child running into the road — the tobidashi bōya ("pop-out boy") traffic warning sign — is so ubiquitous in Japan that it has achieved the paradoxical invisibility of the truly familiar. What very few people know is that every one of these signs traces back to a single source: Shiga Prefecture's Higashiōmi City, where a sign painter named Kudoku began making them in 1973 as a personal contribution to road safety, distributing them at his own expense to intersections near schools. Shiga Prefecture now hosts more than 1,000 of them per square kilometer — more, per capita, than any prefecture in Japan — and has spawned an entire regional cottage industry of variants: local mascot versions, historical character versions, festival-character versions. The origin site in Higashiōmi preserves the original designs alongside the evolutionary tree of 50-plus years of local iteration. This is the origin story of something so omnipresent it stopped being noticed.
highlights_en: A sign painter's personal 1973 campaign to prevent traffic deaths created an icon so successful it colonized the entire country — and almost no one knows it came from here
Shiga Prefecture's tobidashi bōya density is the highest in Japan; walking through certain neighborhoods is like walking through a convention
The local variant ecosystem — Hikone Castle mascot bōya, ancient messenger bōya, festival character bōya — represents 50 years of folk art iteration on a single graphic

summary_en: A converted school building in the hills of Yamagata City, Gifu Prefecture contains 200-plus pieces of Shōwa-era game and vending machine history, most of them operational, all of them representing the specific flavors of entertainment technology that Japan produced and largely abandoned between the 1960s and 1990s. The operative word is "operational": this is not a collection of objects behind glass but a functioning arcade of antique machines in which a 1970s pinball game, a 1980s medal shooter, and — most improbably — a hot-food vending machine dispensing ramen and toast in their original Shōwa configurations can all be played, operated, and consumed during a single visit. The time-based admission system (1,000 yen per hour) creates a specific relationship with the material that conventional admission models do not: you are buying time inside an era rather than access to a collection. For those to whom the retro-Japan aesthetic is not nostalgia but archaeology, the Gifu Retro Museum offers a density of first-hand material that no amount of reading about the period replicates.
highlights_en: Shōwa-era hot-food vending machines — ramen, toast, canned goods — still operational and still selling: the most edible form of time travel available
200-plus vintage arcade and game machines in active operation: a working museum of an entertainment technology that no longer exists outside places like this

summary_en: On a wooded mountainside in Asahi Town, a small Shinto shrine quietly enshrines a deity unlike any other in Japan: the air itself. There is no carved figure, no sacred mirror, no relic at the center of worship — only the invisible substance everyone is already breathing. To make the absent god somehow visible, the shrine's main hall is built as a polished, mirror-finish stainless steel cube set flush with a hillside clearing, its surfaces reflecting the surrounding cedars, the sky, and the visitor's own face back at them. The result is a shrine that disappears into its forest while making the air around it conspicuously present. Conceived in 1990 as a meditation on the environment and the unseen, the Air Shrine sits at the intersection of contemporary art, Shinto tradition, and the older Japanese intuition that the most important things are usually the ones you cannot see. Festival rites here include silent moments of simply breathing in unison — perhaps the most minimal sacred ritual in the country.
highlights_en: A modern Shinto shrine whose object of worship is, literally, the air — no statue, no mirror, only what surrounds you
The mirror-finish stainless steel main hall reflects the surrounding forest, so the architecture half-vanishes into the trees
A rare contemporary fusion of environmental thought, traditional Shinto, and minimalist sculpture, hidden in the Yamagata mountains

summary_en: Rising 120 meters above the Ibaraki plains — three times the height of the Statue of Liberty without her pedestal — the Ushiku Daibutsu is the tallest bronze statue in Japan and one of the tallest standing statues in the world. Completed in 1993 by the Jōdo Shinshū Higashi Honganji sect, it depicts Amida Buddha with one hand raised in the gesture of reassurance, his serene face looking out over the flat farmland for kilometers in every direction. The scale is genuinely difficult to absorb from photographs: the Buddha's eyes alone are a meter wide, and a 5.3-meter Statue of Liberty would fit neatly into the palm of his hand. Visitors can enter the body through the lotus pedestal and ride an elevator 85 meters up to a viewing chamber inside the Buddha's chest, where small windows look out over the Kantō plain. The interior is staged as a quiet pilgrimage — incense, votive halls, thousands of small golden Buddha figures — making the experience equal parts religious site, civil engineering marvel, and roadside wonder. On clear days, the Tokyo Skytree is visible from the chest cavity.
highlights_en: A 120-meter standing bronze Buddha — one of the tallest statues on Earth, looming above farmland visible from kilometers away
Ride an elevator into the Buddha's chest cavity for a viewing chamber 85 meters above the ground, with Tokyo Skytree visible on clear days

summary_en: Tucked into a quiet Meguro side street, the only museum in the world dedicated entirely to parasites occupies two compact floors of dense, unsensational science. Founded in 1953 by parasitologist Satoru Kamegai out of frustration that postwar Japan was rapidly forgetting the public-health crises that parasitic infections had only recently caused, the museum displays roughly 300 specimens drawn from a collection of around 60,000 — flukes, tapeworms, nematodes, and their hosts, all carefully labeled in Japanese and English. The centerpiece is an 8.8-meter tapeworm extracted from a single human patient, suspended in its full length beside a ribbon of equivalent length that visitors can hold to grasp the scale. The tone is rigorously educational, not lurid: parasitology is presented as a real and necessary branch of zoology and medicine, and the gift shop's parasite-themed keychains and T-shirts have the quietly subversive humor of a place that treats its difficult subject with complete seriousness. Admission is free. It has been a Tokyo cult destination for decades — and an unexpectedly popular first-date spot.

summary_en: In the hills outside Komatsu, a 15-meter Buddha head rises from the ground at the entrance to a long, low cavern carved into the hillside, its face the first warning sign that you have arrived somewhere unusual. Hanibe Gankutsuin is the life's work of a single sculptor, Tōjō Dōbutsu (and continued by his son), who from the late 1950s onward populated this cave with several hundred plaster and concrete figures depicting Buddhist cosmology with unusual literalness. Inside, dim lighting illuminates scenes of the eight hells — sinners boiled, flayed, impaled, and devoured by demons — rendered in the same uncanny, hand-shaped style across hundreds of meters of corridor. There are also peaceful tableaux of paradise, bodhisattvas, and folk-religion figures, but it is the hell scenes that visitors remember, partly because they are presented without irony as genuine moral instruction. The complex stays cool year-round and the lighting is deliberately atmospheric; what could be a horror experience instead lands closer to outsider art on a vast scale, the obsessive vision of one artist who decided a cave full of demons was the most useful thing he could leave behind.

summary_en: On the lower slopes of Mount Tate, one of Japan's three sacred peaks, the prefectural Tateyama Museum maintains an experiential outdoor exhibit called Mandara Yūen — a walk-through reconstruction of the cosmology that Tateyama pilgrims once experienced as a literal map of the afterlife. Visitors progress through three contiguous zones: the Hell Garden, with its sulfurous imagery and bleak red-rock pathways evoking the molten ravines that medieval pilgrims really believed lay inside the mountain; the Path of Reincarnation, a transitional forest dotted with sculptures of the six realms; and the Pure Land, an airy white pavilion meant to evoke Amida's western paradise. The piece functions as both a contemporary art installation and a serious historical reconstruction: until the Meiji period, ordinary people came to Tateyama specifically because the mountain was understood to contain hell within its geology, and the journey across these landscapes was a rehearsal for one's own death. Mandara Yūen makes that vanished worldview walkable again, in a setting where the actual sacred mountain looms quietly in the background.

summary_en: Kamijima is a small island in Ise Bay, two thousand inhabitants, no cars, reached by a thirty-minute ferry from Toba and known mainly as the setting for Yukio Mishima's novel The Sound of Waves. Tucked into the cliffs on the island's southeastern side is a relic of a much darker era: a concrete observation post built by the Imperial Japanese Army to monitor the bay during the Second World War, abandoned in 1945 and slowly being reclaimed by salt-spray and vines ever since. Reaching it requires a fifty-minute walk along the island's narrow coastal trail, through pine forests and past tiny shrines, until the rectangular concrete structure appears suddenly at the edge of the sea. From its slit windows the view is breathtaking — open ocean, distant ships, the Atsumi Peninsula on the horizon — and the contrast between that beauty and the weapon-spotting purpose for which the building was constructed is the entire experience. The structure is unfenced and on public land, but the island offers no facilities; this is an observational visit, not a destination.

summary_en: Long before Japan had words like 'industrial heritage,' the village of Niu was already old: ancient sources describe mercury cinnabar being mined here from the Yayoi and Kofun periods onward, and the bright red ore from these hills was used to gild the Great Buddha of Nara in the 8th century. The mine continued, on and off, into the 1970s, leaving a scattered landscape of adits, slag heaps, and weather-worn machinery distributed across the forested slopes of southern Mie. Most of the workings are sealed or unsafe to enter, but the surface features — collapsing wooden head-frames, narrow rail beds, stone-walled retaining terraces — can be observed from the village's mountain road, where a few interpretive signs explain the site's relationship to the gilding of the Nara Daibutsu and to centuries of Shingon Buddhist alchemical practice that depended on cinnabar. For visitors interested in the deep, unbroken industrial threads that connect ancient temple-building to modern industry, the Niu mercury workings are one of the most evocative sites in central Japan, precisely because so little of them has been packaged for tourism.
highlights_en: Mercury cinnabar from these hills was used to gild the Great Buddha of Nara in the 8th century — a direct material link between Mie and ancient capital architecture

summary_en: Known locally and affectionately as Okashira-san — 'Mr. Head' — Kōbe-no-Miya Yomo Shrine is one of the few shrines in Japan whose spiritual jurisdiction is, specifically, the human head. The deity enshrined here is said to grant blessings for everything that occurs above the neck: scholarship, mental clarity, recovery from headaches and brain illness, the lifting of curses, hair restoration, exam success, and — increasingly in the social-media era — protection for athletes whose sports involve the head. The shrine's grounds are quiet and forested, in a remote corner of southern Mie's Taiki Town, and the votive plaques (ema) are dense with extremely specific prayers from students, surgeons, headache sufferers, and the occasional balding pilgrim. The shrine's foundation legend involves the head of a Heian-period nobleman that, according to local tradition, was washed up by a flooded river and enshrined here. The official literature describes Kōbe-no-Miya as 'the only shrine of its kind in Japan,' a claim that has been repeated for so long it functions as a piece of folk truth in its own right.

summary_en: On the southern coast of the Shima Peninsula, two boulders face each other across roughly fifty meters of forested slope, and between them an acoustic curiosity has been quietly demonstrating itself for centuries. At one rock (the 'speaking spot'), an ordinary speaking voice — neither raised nor projected — is precisely transmitted across the gap to the other rock (the 'listening spot'), where it can be heard with full clarity, including soft consonants and changes in tone. The effect is the product of the boulders' specific shapes, their angle to each other, and the natural amphitheater of the slope between them, and once you have walked from one rock to the other to test the phenomenon yourself, it remains difficult to believe even after repeated trials. Local folklore treats the site with the respect ordinarily reserved for shrines: prayers, secrets, and confessions have been spoken into Oumu-iwa for generations, the listening rock acting as something between an oracle and a sacred ear. Approach the path carefully — the woods are unimproved and slippery after rain — but the experiment itself takes only a few minutes and lodges permanently in memory.

summary_en: Up a winding mountain road in Toba, past the last houses and the last asphalt, a small Shinto site centered on a clear waterfall offers one of the more accessible introductions to taki-gyō — waterfall ascetic practice — that exists in mainland Japan. Shirataki Daimyōjin venerates the falls themselves as kami, in the older Japanese tradition in which natural features (rocks, trees, water) are not symbols of the sacred but the sacred itself. With prior arrangement, visitors may participate in misogi purification under the cold mountain water, a brief but serious ritual in which one wades waist-deep into the basin, intones a purification prayer, and stands under the falling water long enough to lose track of breath. The practice is not packaged as adventure tourism; the priests treat it as religious practice and expect the same from participants. For those not undertaking the rite, the site itself — pure mountain water, mossy boulders, simple wooden torii — is one of the more unaffected sacred spaces in the Ise-Shima region, and a reminder of what most Japanese shrines were before they were buildings.
highlights_en: A still-active center for taki-gyō waterfall ascetic practice — visitors can arrange to undertake the cold-water purification ritual with the resident priest

summary_en: Every autumn in the Iinan district of Matsusaka, a local committee constructs a single enormous figure entirely out of rice straw — six meters tall, up to eleven meters wide, built around a wooden frame by volunteers in the weeks after the rice harvest. summary_en: Seki was the forty-seventh post station on the Tōkaidō, the old highway connecting Edo and Kyoto, and at each end of its preserved Edo-period main street stands a 'fork' (oiwake) — the precise spot where the Tōkaidō branched off toward other routes, marked since at least the 17th century by stone lanterns, road markers, and (in the eastern case) a great wooden torii gate pointing toward Ise Grand Shrine. The Eastern Fork sends pilgrims south down the Ise Branch Road toward Ise Jingū, and its torii — replaced every twenty years to coincide with the Grand Shrine's ritual rebuilding — visibly marks the start of that sacred southern journey. The Western Fork sends travelers west along the Yamato Road into the Nara basin. Walking from one fork to the other through the preserved town is the most economical way to grasp how Japanese post stations actually worked: not as static villages but as junctions, with their identity defined as much by the roads leaving them as by the buildings inside.

summary_en: Deep in the upper reaches of the Sekisuikei ravine, in the Suzuka Mountains west of Kameyama, a small stone Kannon statue is enshrined inside a natural rock grotto, and a thin, slender waterfall called Kiyotaki ('Pure Falls') drops down the cliff face beside it. The combination of cave shrine and waterfall is a textbook example of Japanese mountain religion — water and stone elevated to the status of divinity, a Buddhist Kannon installed inside the natural form rather than in a built structure — and the site has functioned as a pilgrimage stop for at least several centuries. summary_en: At the tip of the Shima Peninsula, on the beach at Goza, a small stone Buddha sits at the water's edge — and twice a day, at high tide, vanishes beneath the sea. At low tide, the figure re-emerges, salt-stained and slightly weathered, and the local women of Goza walk down to make offerings, particularly for ailments of the lower body and reproductive health, for which the Shio-botoke ('Tidal Buddha') is said to grant specific blessings. The phenomenon — a sacred image that performs its own daily drowning and resurrection — has made the Goza Buddha one of the most quietly powerful folk-religion sites in coastal Japan. The site is not signposted as a tourist attraction; it sits inside the living space of an active fishing village, surrounded by the homes of ama divers and small boats drawn up on the sand. name_en: Kongōshō-ji Okunoin (Stupa-Lined Inner Sanctuary of Asama Peak)
summary_en: Kongōshō-ji sits atop Mount Asama, the peak that guards the northeast — the unlucky 'demon gate' direction — of Ise Grand Shrine, and a centuries-old proverb still circulates in Ise: 'A pilgrimage to Ise that doesn't include Asama is only half a pilgrimage.' Beyond the temple's main hall, a forested path climbs further to the okunoin, the inner sanctuary, and it is on this path that visitors encounter one of the most unusual sacred landscapes in Japan: a corridor lined with tens of thousands of towering wooden stupas (sotoba), each erected by a bereaved family in memory of a deceased relative. The Ise-Shima region has a unique funeral custom (take-mairi) in which families ascend Mount Asama in the weeks after a death and plant a large stupa here, often three or more meters tall, leaving the dead in the care of the mountain. The cumulative effect — a forest of inscribed wooden posts, weathering at different rates, packed densely along the path — is one of the most moving expressions of Japanese mortuary practice still visibly active in the 21st century. Treat with reverence; this is a living funerary site, not a sightseeing curiosity.

summary_en: In the ama-diver village of Ōsatsu, on the Toba coast, a small stone statue of Ebisu — the laughing fisherman-god of fortune and the sea — sits at the edge of the harbor with most of its nose missing. summary_en: On a small hill in Tōkai City stands a quietly remarkable Buddha: 18.79 meters tall, made of reinforced concrete, completed in 1927 to commemorate the wedding of the future Shōwa Emperor — a private gift to the public from a Nagoya businessman who paid for it out of his own pocket. summary_en: Across the causeway from the sacred island of Takeshima in Gamagōri stands what its owners call 'the only seashell museum in the world,' though that undersells what is actually inside. summary_en: In a quiet residential temple district in eastern Nagoya, a 10-meter bronze Buddha sits cross-legged in the precincts of Tōgan-ji — and the statue is, unmistakably, bright green. summary_en: In Seto, one of Japan's six ancient pottery towns and a major historical producer of maneki-neko (the beckoning cats that summon customers from every Japanese shop window), a private museum holds one of the country's largest collections devoted to the figure. summary_en: In a quiet residential block in Kōnan City, an 18-meter concrete Buddha sits in the front yard of an ordinary suburban house. The Hotei Daibutsu was built between 1949 and 1954 by Maeda Hidenobu, a local acupuncturist who experienced a dream in which the Buddha appeared to him and asked to be made physical. Maeda spent five years and most of his savings building the figure on his own land, two meters taller than the Great Buddha of Nara, and the statue has now sat sandwiched between a railway level-crossing and an ordinary street ever since — possibly the largest private-individual-commissioned Buddha in Japan. In recent years the figure has gone viral on Japanese social media under a new name: the 'Sunglasses Buddha,' because the warning lights of the adjacent railway crossing, when activated, align almost exactly with the Buddha's eyes and appear to give him a pair of glowing rectangular shades. The phenomenon is best photographed at sundown when a train is due. The Buddha remains a private structure on residential property; observe from the public road only, do not block the crossing, and remember that you are, in effect, photographing a stranger's front garden.

summary_en: Inside an unassuming temple hall in central Gifu, a 13.63-meter seated Shaka Buddha presides as one of the strangest engineering achievements in Japanese Buddhist art — and the largest dry-lacquer-and-paper Buddha in Japan. Construction began in 1791 by the temple's eleventh abbot as a memorial for victims of the great famines and earthquakes that had devastated Gifu in the late 18th century. The frame was built around the trunk of an enormous ginkgo tree; over the trunk, a basket-like cage was woven from bamboo; on the bamboo, clay was applied; over the clay, approximately 40,000 paper copies of Buddhist sutras handwritten on Mino washi were pasted, layer after layer; and the whole was finally finished in lacquer and gold leaf. The technique — called the kago, or 'basket,' construction — has no real parallel anywhere else, and the Buddha himself sits, lightweight and luminous, inside a temple barely wider than his shoulders. Designated a Cultural Property of Gifu Prefecture in 1974, the Gifu Daibutsu is sometimes counted as one of Japan's three great Buddhas, alongside Nara and Kamakura.

summary_en: Beneath the main hall of Seki Zenkō-ji — a small Tendai temple in the cutlery town of Seki — runs the only known kaidan meguri ('precept-platform pilgrimage') in Japan laid out in the shape of a Buddhist manji (the swastika that is one of the oldest symbols of the dharma). The corridor is 49 meters long — exactly the 49 days of the bardo between death and rebirth in Buddhist cosmology — and the visitor enters by descending into a pitch-black underground passage, holding a rope along the left wall, and feeling forward in total darkness. Somewhere in the dark hangs a metal lock said to be the 'key to paradise'; touching it is the spiritual climax of the rite, and the only way to find it is by patient touch in absolute blackness. The disorientation produced by walking blind through a swastika-shaped corridor at the precise length of the 49-day bardo is, by design, a controlled rehearsal of death and rebirth. Visitors with claustrophobia or heart conditions should not attempt it; everyone else should expect a few minutes of complete sensory deprivation followed by a quietly altered state of mind.

name_en: Kanayama Megaliths / Iwaya Iwakage Site (Japan's Stonehenge)
summary_en: In the wooded hills of Gero's Kanayama district, a scatter of enormous granite boulders has been arranged — or, the more cautious researchers say, naturally placed — in a configuration that appears to function as a Stone Age solar calendar. On the days of the autumnal-equinox-adjacent festival of frost (Sōkō, around October 23) and the late-winter festival of melting (Usui, around February 19), sunlight at a specific moment in the afternoon passes through a narrow gap between the megaliths and strikes a precise spot inside a cave-like structure called the Iwaya Iwakage. Below the rocks, excavation has yielded stone arrowheads and pottery from the Jōmon period some 8,000 years ago, alongside artifacts continuing into the Edo era. The site was designated a Prefectural Historic Site in 1973. Above the megaliths sits the small shrine Iwaya Iwa-jinja, which incorporates the Heian-era legend of the warrior Akugenta Yoshihira slaying a hihi monkey-monster here, layering Stone Age archaeology, prehistoric astronomy, medieval folklore, and active local Shinto into a single hillside. Local volunteer guides run interpretive tours and are by far the best way to grasp the site.
highlights_en: A scatter of granite megaliths arranged so that sunlight passes through a precise gap and strikes a specific spot inside a cave on the days of Sōkō and Usui — possibly an 8,000-year-old solar calendar

summary_en: A long stretch of the Kani River in eastern Gifu cuts through one of Japan's largest exposed granite formations — house-sized boulders, fissured cliffs, and sculpted natural arches that have been weathering into ever-stranger shapes for millennia. Designated a National Place of Scenic Beauty and Natural Monument in 1934, Oniiwa ('Demon Rock') Park takes its name from a Heian-period legend: a demon called Seki-no-Tarō was said to live in these boulders, and the local festival held every Setsubun (around February 3) reverses the standard Japanese bean-throwing chant. Where most communities throw beans while shouting 'Demons out, fortune in,' the people of Oniiwa shout 'Demons in, fortune in' — because in their version of the story, the demon, once driven out, returned as a benevolent god and is now welcomed back. The park's walking trails climb among the boulders with rope ladders and chained pitches; a hot spring district adjoins the entrance. The geology, the legend, and the inverted bean-throwing ritual together produce one of the most distinctive folk-religion landscapes in the Tōkai region.

summary_en: At roughly 900 meters elevation in the foothills of the Northern Alps, Japan's highest-altitude show cave snakes nearly 800 meters into a mountainside, divided into three sections (each with its own exit) so visitors can choose a 10-, 20- or 30-minute experience. The cave's signature features are the eerie blue-lit subterranean streams, a chamber called Moon World, an unusually dense population of helictites (twisted stalactites that defy gravity by growing sideways), 'Japan's largest column,' and a final cascade called the Falls of Happiness. The cave's discoverer and developer, the late Ōhashi Sotokichi, was also a compulsive private collector of minerals, gems, and decorative art from around the world, and beside the cave entrance he built a private museum to house his finds. The Ōhashi Collection Hall sits awkwardly and wonderfully against the cave proper — geological showpiece next to private cabinet of curiosities — making this one of the more characteristic outsider-natural-history complexes in central Japan. Year-round 10°C, so a jacket is essential even in midsummer.
highlights_en: Japan's highest-altitude show cave at 900 meters, nearly 800 meters long, with three sections and three exits so visitors can choose their depth

summary_en: On a hillside in suburban northern Sendai, a 100-meter white Kannon — the bodhisattva of compassion — rises out of the woods, visible from the Tōhoku Expressway and from JR train windows kilometers away. Completed in 1991 to commemorate the centennial of the city of Sendai, the figure is among the tallest statues in the world, with 21 additional meters of structure descending below ground inside the base. The cumulative effect is a complete, walk-through Buddhist cosmology compressed inside a 100-meter white statue at the edge of a Japanese suburb — one of the country's purest examples of postwar 'colossal religious landmark' culture, still active as a place of pilgrimage and increasingly photographed as a piece of weird modern architecture.

summary_en: At the foot of Mount Senganmori — a strangely conical, near-pyramidal peak that has been a UFO-sighting hot spot since the 1970s — sits one of the only municipally operated UFO museums in Japan. summary_en: B-Hōkan — roughly, 'Museum of B-Grade Treasures' — is the private museum of economist and television commentator Morinaga Takurō, opened in 2014 in a small three-story concrete building in suburban Tokorozawa. The official tagline is 'a poor, foolish, but beautiful museum,' and the contents make good on the promise: hundreds of thousands of items of mass-produced postwar Japanese consumer flotsam, painstakingly categorized and displayed as the social history of a particular country between roughly 1950 and the present. Glico caramel-box prizes are arranged by year. Plastic milk-bottle caps are sorted by region. Kinnikuman gum erasers, empty cigarette packs, vintage matchbox labels, and 1970s soft-drink cans are filed by manufacturer. The argument is the same throughout: that which the consumer society throws away is the actual record of how the consumer society lived, and one obsessive economist with a working knowledge of taxonomy can flip 'trash' into 'archive' simply by classifying it correctly. Open by appointment only; small, residential, and one of the strangest serious arguments for what a museum can be in the country.

summary_en: In the mountains of Katsuyama, far enough from anywhere else that the first glimpse of it from the access road is genuinely startling, a 17-meter seated Buddha sits inside a colossal modern temple hall, surrounded by a 75-meter five-story pagoda, a long covered cloister, a stroll garden with ponds, and approximately 1,281 smaller Buddhas distributed across the precinct. The entire complex was built between 1987 and the early 1990s by a single individual — Tada Kiyoshi, the founder of a local taxi company — who funded the project from his own fortune with the explicit ambition of building a temple larger than Nara. He succeeded: the seated Buddha is several meters taller than the great Buddha of Tōdai-ji, and the surrounding pagoda is one of the tallest in Japan. The complex never achieved the visitor numbers it was built for, and there is now something melancholy and grand about wandering its enormous emptiness. With the recent extension of the Hokuriku Shinkansen to Fukui, the temple is being slowly rediscovered as one of the country's most concentrated examples of single-patron sacred architecture.
highlights_en: A 17-meter Buddha and a 75-meter pagoda commissioned and funded entirely by one taxi-company founder in the late 1980s — possibly the most ambitious private-patron temple project in modern Japan

summary_en: The Iwashita Shin-Shōga Museum is what happens when a 19th-century pickle company decides to build the world's first museum dedicated entirely to its single most famous product: young pickled ginger. Opened in 2015 by Iwashita Foods in their home town of Tochigi, the museum is, top to bottom, ferociously pink: walls, ceilings, light fixtures, exhibits, cafeteria, mascot character (Iwashika-chan), even the in-house Shintō-style 'Ginger Shrine' where visitors can pray for ginger-related wishes. Permanent exhibits cover the history of ginger, the manufacturing process, vintage packaging from every decade since the 1950s, and a rotating series of crossover events with anime franchises, idol groups, and contemporary artists. The on-site cafe Pink Deli serves food in which essentially every dish includes new ginger as an ingredient — including ginger soft-serve, ginger curry, and ginger soda. Admission is free; photography is encouraged throughout; and the museum has become, against expectation, one of the surprise pilgrimage sites of provincial Japanese subculture tourism.

summary_en: On a low hill on the island of Shōdoshima in the Seto Inland Sea, a tall white standing Kannon — locally called the Shiawase Kannon, or 'Happiness Kannon' — rises above olive groves and small farms. The figure won first prize at a French international contest of architectural artworks (the so-called 'Arc Plus' competition), an unusual pedigree for a Japanese roadside Buddha and the reason the island's tourism agency cheerfully promotes the statue as 'the world's most beautiful Kannon.' Inside the statue's hollow body, an elevator carries visitors up through galleries holding 11,000 small votive Buddhas to a viewing chamber located inside the figure's chest, where windows look out across the Inland Sea toward Tonoshō Port and the famous Angel Road sandbar. Relics of the historical Buddha, donated from Sri Lanka, are enshrined in the chest gallery. At night, the figure is illuminated and visible from passing ferries — one of the small constellation of unexpected landmarks that makes Shōdoshima feel, at every turn, like a larger island than its map suggests.

summary_en: In the snow country of the Shōnai region, at the foot of the sacred Mount Yudono, the temple of Dainichibō has cared for the same congregation for over a thousand years — and at the center of its main hall sits its most famous member, the mummified body of the monk Shinnyokai-Shōnin, who entered sokushinbutsu ('living Buddhahood') in 1783 at the age of 96. The path that led him to this state is among the most extreme ascetic traditions in world religion: years of mokujikigyō (a diet of bark, roots, nuts, and pine needles, eliminating all grains) progressively dehydrated his body in life; long stretches of solitary meditation hollowed his metabolism; finally, while still alive, he was sealed underground in a stone chamber, breathing through a bamboo tube and chanting sutras until breath stopped. Three years later, his preserved body was disinterred and enshrined as a sokushinbutsu. He has been receiving visitors ever since. The temple treats him not as a curiosity but as a living priest still performing the same intercessory function he intended in 1783, and visitors are asked to behave as worshippers, not spectators. He is one of roughly sixteen sokushinbutsu still extant, the great majority of them in this small region of Yamagata.
highlights_en: The mummified body of Shinnyokai-Shōnin (1687-1783), who entered living Buddhahood through years of bark-and-pine-needle ascetic diet before being sealed underground while still alive

summary_en: In the Naguri mountains north of Hannō, a single Saitama businessman named Hiranuma Yatarō (1892-1979) spent decades of the postwar reconstruction era building his own private 300,000-tsubo (roughly 100-hectare) Buddhist mountain. The Torii Kannon complex includes a main hall, a great bell tower, a 13-story pagoda dedicated to the relics of the 7th-century Chinese monk Xuanzang (whose travels to India inspired Journey to the West), a 33-meter white Kannon of Salvation on the summit, a Peace Kannon, a Shaka Buddha image, and a network of pilgrimage paths winding among them all. summary_en: For about forty days each autumn (October 23 to November 30), the temple of Chōgaku-ji on the Yamanobe-no-Michi — Japan's oldest documented road — unrolls a set of nine large painted scrolls in its main hall. The Daijigokue, or Great Hell Scrolls, date from the Edo period and depict, with extraordinary visual force, the full Buddhist cosmology of postmortem judgment: the Ten Kings of Hell presiding over their tribunals, the old hag Datsue-ba stripping the dead at the Sanzu River, the Eight Great Hells (boiling, knife-edged, crushing, screaming, twice-screaming, scorching, twice-scorching, and the endless avici), and finally the Pure Land of Amida. On weekend afternoons during the opening, the head priest performs etoki — the medieval Japanese practice of 'picture-explaining,' walking visitors through the scrolls as a vivid morality drama. Etoki is a living oral tradition that has nearly died out elsewhere; here it continues in the soft autumn light, with the same scrolls that Edo-period villagers stared at five generations ago. summary_en: In the village of Kamo, in coastal Anan, a small Shinto shrine has, over four centuries, absorbed approximately ten thousand maneki-neko statues offered by petitioners praying for victory in legal disputes, court cases, and contests of every kind. summary_en: In the coastal city of Uwajima, on Shikoku's western edge, a branch shrine of the great Taga Shrine of Ōmi maintains an adjoining 'Folk Cultural Property Museum' (Dekoboko Shindō, literally 'Hall of the Uneven Gods') devoted to the folk-religious symbolism of sexuality. The collection has been built up over generations by votive donation: Edo-period shunga (erotic woodblock prints) and ukiyo-e, carved wooden and stone phalli and vulvae, fertility folk-art from across Japan, ema votive plaques inscribed with prayers for conception and matrimonial harmony, and curiosities from foreign sex-cultures collected by previous priests. Taga is one of the few major shrines in Japan whose stated purview includes longevity, healing, childbirth, and marital fertility, and the museum exists to make that traditional purview material rather than coy. Entry is restricted to visitors over 18; the curation is matter-of-fact and the framing is anthropological rather than titillating. For visitors interested in the older Japanese view of human reproduction as religious rather than embarrassing, the Dekoboko Shindō is among the most concentrated collections in the country.

summary_en: Up a mountain road in the woods of Karakawa-chō, outside Izumo, a small shrine of striking antiquity is recorded in both the 733 Izumo no Kuni Fudoki and the 927 Engishiki — making it one of the oldest documented shrines in Japan. The name 'Karakama' means 'Korean cauldron,' a reference to the iron-and-cauldron technology associated with Silla and absorbed into the deep iron-smelting culture of Izumo. To reach the main shrine, pilgrims climb about three hundred uneven stone steps, and then — just before the shrine itself — squeeze through a 45-centimeter gap between two huge boulders, an authentic test of body and intent. No cell signal, no signage, no concessions to the casual visitor; the mountain forest and the gap in the rock are the entire experience.

summary_en: On the western slopes of Mount Fuji, a lava cave called Hitoana ('the Human Hole') has been understood since at least the 13th century as a literal entrance to the realm of the kami of Fuji — the great Sengen Daibosatsu — and as a portal between the world of the living and the world of the dead. In the early 17th century, the cave became the meditation retreat of Hasegawa Kakugyō, the founder of the Fujikō pilgrim associations, who is said to have spent extended periods inside in austere training. From the 18th century onward, as the Fujikō movement spread among Edo townsfolk, ordinary pilgrims began leaving inscribed stone stelae outside the cave entrance to mark their visits, their prayers, and their dead. More than two hundred such stelae remain today, dating from across two centuries of working-class religious practice, set in a small ravine around the cave mouth. The site is administered by Fujinomiya City; access to the cave interior is by reservation through the local museum, and the surface stelae can be visited freely outside winter.

name_en: Funatsu Tainai Jukei (Womb-Cave Lava Tree Mold)
summary_en: When lava from one of Mount Fuji's eruptions engulfed a living tree, the wood eventually burned away and left behind a long, sinuous cavity in the cooled stone — a tree-shaped tunnel in the lava itself. At Funatsu, this kind of cavity was reinterpreted by Fujikō pilgrims as a 'tainai' (womb), and entering and exiting through the narrow opening became a ritual of symbolic rebirth, performed by pilgrims on the day before climbing Mount Fuji to purify the body and start the ascent anew. The interior walls are striated with rib-like patterns formed where bark once stood; the local pilgrims interpreted these as the literal ribcage of the mother goddess Sengen Daibosatsu, completing the womb metaphor with anatomical specificity. The cave is a designated Natural Monument, administered today by Fujikawaguchiko Town; admission is modest, the cave is electrically lit but very narrow, and the experience of squeezing through the constriction and emerging into open air is one of the most unforgettable small rituals available on the Fuji circuit.

name_en: Mount Osore (Reijō Osorezan, Sacred Mountain of the Dead)
summary_en: On the Shimokita Peninsula at the northern tip of Honshū, an active volcanic caldera holds one of Japan's three most sacred mountains for the dead. Mount Osore is a yellow-gray landscape of sulfur vents, bubbling hot springs, and bone-white pumice fields, ringed by the milky-blue Lake Usori, and Buddhist tradition has overlaid these features so completely with the geography of the afterlife that the walk through them functions as a kind of dress rehearsal for one's own dying. A small bridge crossing a stream is identified as the Sanzu River, the boundary that the dead must cross. Beyond it, the Eight Great Hells unfold across the actual volcanic terrain: rocks become Datsue-ba and the demons of judgment, sulfur vents become hell-mouths, and the cracked moonscape near the central temple is the Sai-no-Kawara, the dry riverbed where the souls of dead children stack stones in penance — except here the stones really are stacked, in vast quiet drifts, by living parents and grandparents memorializing real losses. Pinwheels turn in the wind beside them. The mountain is open from May to October; treat the entire experience as funerary rather than touristic.
highlights_en: An active volcanic caldera mapped point-for-point onto the Buddhist landscape of the afterlife — Sanzu River, Eight Hells, Sai-no-Kawara, Pure Land beach

summary_en: On the outskirts of Kurume, in Fukuoka Prefecture, a regional branch of the famous Narita-san temple complex maintains one of the more theatrically committed hell experiences in Japanese Buddhism. The Jigokukan ('Hell Hall') is a walk-through diorama of the Eight Great Hells of Buddhist cosmology — Black Rope, Crushing, Screaming, Twice-Screaming, Scorching, Twice-Scorching, Reviving, and the endless avici — each rendered as a separate room with life-sized figures of demons inflicting period-appropriate torments on the damned, accompanied by sound effects and selective lighting that genuinely raise the heart rate. The Hell Hall is positioned within a larger pilgrimage circuit that includes a vast Merciful Mother Kannon, a Peace Pagoda containing a Pure Land hall, and a Filial Piety Cave — moving the visitor through fear, mercy, and gratitude in roughly that order. The intent is moral instruction in the medieval Japanese pattern: see the hells in physical detail, then experience the consolation of paradise. Allow an hour for the full circuit and bring children old enough to know that the demons are not real.

summary_en: Mara Kannon is a small wayside shrine in the hot-spring district of Tawarayama, Nagato, where the local story begins in tragedy. When the warlord Ouchi Yoshitaka was overthrown in 1551, his young heir was reportedly disguised as a girl and smuggled into hiding here, only to be discovered, captured, and killed. It is best understood not as a roadside curiosity but as a layering of mourning, lineage, and fertility belief — and depicted with that in mind.

A nationally rare granite outcrop showing classic 'onion-skin' spheroidal weathering
An iwakura-style sacred space deep in the precincts of Itsukushima Shrine

name: 霊巌寺の奇岩
name_kana: れいがんじのきがん
address: 福岡県八女市黒木町笠原9731
summary: 八女市黒木町の霊巌寺境内にそびえる県指定天然記念物の奇岩群。市公式は、座禅岩、女岩、仲人岩、仏法岩、剣岩、犬岩、猫岩といった名を挙げ、なかでも高さ12m余の男岩は日本最大級と説明する。寺院・修験・奇岩名・性象徴が重なり、資料館色のない自然信仰系候補として強い。
highlights: 座禅岩、女岩、仲人岩、剣岩、犬岩、猫岩など名を持つ奇岩群
高さ12m余の男岩は日本最大級とされる
八女茶発祥地の古刹と修験的な霊地性が重なる
from_kameyama: 車で約520分（新名神→山陽道→九州道）
summary_en: Within the precincts of Reigan-ji in Kuroki-machi, Yame, stand a prefecturally designated cluster of strange rocks. The city's official page names individual stones — Zazen-iwa (Meditation Rock), Onna-iwa (Woman Rock), Nakodo-iwa (Matchmaker Rock), Buppo-iwa, Tsurugi-iwa (Sword Rock), Inu-iwa (Dog Rock), Neko-iwa (Cat Rock) — and notes that the Otoko-iwa (Man Rock), over 12 m tall, is said to be among the largest in Japan. Temple, Shugendo ascetic associations, named formations, and sexual symbolism overlap in a strong nature-faith candidate without a museum framing.
highlights_en: Named formations including Zazen, Woman, Matchmaker, Sword, Dog, and Cat Rocks
The Otoko-iwa (Man Rock), over 12 m tall, said to be among the largest in Japan
An ancient temple in the birthplace of Yame tea, overlapping with a Shugendo sacred site

name: 耕三寺 千佛洞地獄峡
name_kana: こうさんじ せんぶつどうじごくきょう
address: 広島県尾道市瀬戸田町瀬戸田553-2
summary: 瀬戸田の耕三寺にある全長350mの洞窟型地獄・極楽表現。公式ページでは、源信『往生要集』を視覚で体感するため、富士山の溶岩と浅間山の焼石で岩組みし、約千体の石仏と彫刻絵で十界の場面を表したものと説明される。資料館ではなく『地獄洞窟』として切り出すと、全国版の地獄系スポットに合う。
highlights: 横洞350m・最深部15mの洞窟型地獄極楽空間
約千体の石仏と彫刻絵で十界を表現
富士山溶岩と浅間山焼石で岩組みされた人工洞窟
from_kameyama: 車で約300分（新名神→山陽道→しまなみ海道）
name_en: Kosan-ji — Senbutsudo Jigokukyo (Cave of a Thousand Buddhas)
summary_en: Inside Kosan-ji on Setoda, a 350-meter cave passage stages the hells and paradises of Buddhist cosmology in physical form. The temple's official page describes how, to let visitors experience Genshin's Ojo-Yoshu through sight, the cavern was built up with lava from Mt. Fuji and burnt stones from Mt. Asama, with roughly a thousand stone Buddhas and relief carvings enacting the Ten Realms. Rather than framing the whole complex as a museum, the listing focuses on this hell-cavern as a singular grotto installation.
highlights_en: A 350-meter horizontal cave passage of hells and paradises, descending up to 15 m
Roughly a thousand stone Buddhas and relief carvings depicting the Ten Realms
Cavern walls built from Mt. Fuji lava and Mt. Asama burnt stone

name: 牛伏寺 地獄めぐり回廊
name_kana: ごふくじ じごくめぐりかいろう
address: 長野県松本市内田2573
hours: 受付時間9:00〜17:00目安、地獄回廊は要確認
summary: 松本市内田の古刹・牛伏寺にある地獄めぐり回廊。ローカル報道では、約200年前から伝わる木像で地獄の様子を表現する回廊が2022年に完成したとされ、仁王門脇の回廊に奪衣婆や獄卒などの像が並ぶと紹介される。公式ページで回廊単体の情報が薄いため、追加時は公開条件・撮影可否の再確認を前提にしたい。
highlights: 約200年前から伝わる木像で地獄を表現する回廊
奪衣婆や獄卒などの像が並ぶ地獄めぐり
厄除観音として知られる古刹の中にある異色の造形
from_kameyama: 車で約260分（東名阪→中央道→長野道）
summary_en: A 'hell-tour' corridor inside the ancient temple of Gofuku-ji in Uchida, Matsumoto. Local reporting describes a corridor — completed in 2022 — that uses wooden images handed down for some 200 years to depict the hells, with figures such as Datsue-ba (the old woman who strips the dead) and the hell wardens lined up along a passage beside the Nio gate. Because the temple's own pages give the corridor only sparse coverage, opening hours and photography conditions should be confirmed again before any visit.
highlights_en: A corridor that depicts the hells using wooden images handed down for about 200 years
Figures of Datsue-ba and hell wardens lined along the passage
A striking devotional installation inside a temple long revered as a yakuyoke Kannon site

name: 川倉賽の河原地蔵尊
name_kana: かわくらさいのかわらじぞうそん
address: 青森県五所川原市金木町川倉七夕野426-1
hours: 9:00〜13:00目安、12〜3月休業。大祭時期は混雑に注意
summary: 芦野公園の北東にある小高い丘に、大小約2,000体の地蔵が祀られる霊場。五所川原市公式では、恐山と同様にイタコの霊媒で知られ、旧暦6月22日から24日の例大祭には口寄せを聞く参詣者で賑わうと説明される。賽の河原信仰、死者供養、イタコ文化を一体で扱える津軽の濃い民俗信仰スポット。
highlights: 大小約2,000体の地蔵が集まる霊場
例大祭でイタコの口寄せが行われる
恐山と並び語られる津軽の二大イタコ聖地
from_kameyama: 車で約900分（東名阪→北陸道→日本海東北道→東北道）
summary_en: A sacred site on a low hill northeast of Ashino Park where roughly 2,000 Jizō statues of every size are enshrined. Goshogawara City explains that, like Mt. Osore, the place is known for mediumship by itako shamans, and that during the festival of the 22nd–24th of the sixth lunar month worshippers fill the site to hear the dead spoken through their voices. A dense Tsugaru-region folk shrine where Sai-no-Kawara belief, memorial rites for the dead, and itako culture all converge.
highlights_en: A sacred ground gathering some 2,000 Jizō statues of all sizes
Itako spirit-summoning performed at the great festival
One of Tsugaru's two great itako sanctuaries, spoken of alongside Mt. Osore

name: 真駒内滝野霊園（頭大仏・モアイ像）
name_kana: まこまないたきのれいえん（あたまだいぶつ・もあいぞう）
address: 北海道札幌市南区滝野2
fee: 園内見学は無料、頭大仏殿は拝観寄付金あり
summary: 公益社団法人が運営する巨大公園霊園に、モアイ像、ストーンヘンジ、六地蔵、観音像、安藤忠雄設計の頭大仏殿が並ぶ。公式によれば1981年開園で東京ドーム約20個分の広大な敷地を持ち、大型のモアイ像は高さ9.5m・重さ120t、頭大仏殿は高さ13.5m・重さ1,500tの大仏の頭だけが丘から突き出す独自形式となっている。霊園でありながら巨大モニュメント群が点在するスケール感が異様。
highlights: 高さ9.5m級のモアイ像が並ぶ正門周辺
安藤忠雄設計の丘に包まれた頭大仏殿
霊園内にストーンヘンジや世界各国のモニュメントが点在
from_kameyama: 車＋フェリー約18時間 / 飛行機＋レンタカー約5時間（中部国際空港→新千歳）
summary_en: A vast public-park cemetery, run by a public-interest body, where moai statues, a stonehenge, six Jizō, Kannon images and the Tadao Andō-designed Atama Daibutsu (Head Buddha) hall stand side by side. Per the official site, the larger moai reach 9.5 m tall and 120 t, and the Head Buddha hall is 13.5 m high and weighs 1,500 t, with only the giant Buddha's head emerging from a hill. A modern memorial space whose scale and mash-up of monuments is genuinely uncanny.
highlights_en: Moai statues up to about 9.5 m tall lining the main gate
The Tadao Andō-designed Atama Daibutsu, its head rising from a hill
Stonehenge and monuments from around the world scattered across the cemetery grounds

name: 蜂天国
name_kana: はちてんごく
address: 長野県東御市加沢435-1
fee: 大人300円、中高生100円、小学生以下無料
summary: 世界初のスズメバチの芸術館を名乗る私設展示施設。公式サイトでは、奇作・傑作600点余の蜂の巣を展示すると説明される。蜂の生態を利用しながら、巨大な巣を造形物として見せる発想が強烈で、自然物・執念・B級展示が重なる。経営母体は隣接の生コン会社（塩沢グループ）で、8〜10月には実際の巣作りの様子も観察できる。
highlights: スズメバチの巣を使った世界初の蜂芸術館
奇作・傑作600点余の蜂の巣展示
8〜10月は実際の巣作りを観察可能
from_kameyama: 車で約300分（東名阪→中央道→長野道→上信越道）
summary_en: A privately run exhibition hall that bills itself as the world's first 'art museum of hornet nests'. The official site states that some 600-plus extraordinary hornet-nest works are on display. The idea of treating giant hornet nests — built by the hornets themselves — as sculptural objects is striking, sitting at the intersection of natural form, sheer obsession, and B-class display. It is run by an affiliated ready-mix concrete company, and from August through October real nest-building can also be observed.
highlights_en: The self-styled world's first art museum of hornet nests
Some 600-plus extraordinary hornet-nest works on display
Real nest-building visible from August through October

name: 西生寺（即身仏と雷獣のミイラ）
name_kana: さいしょうじ（そくしんぶつとらいじゅうのみいら）
address: 新潟県長岡市寺泊野積8996
fee: 大人・高校生500円、小中学生300円
hours: 受付9:00〜15:30、12月中旬〜3月末は冬期休観
summary: 弥彦山中腹の古刹に、弘智法印の即身仏が祀られる。公式サイトでは、弘智法印が3,000日に及ぶ修行ののち貞治2年(1363年)に御入定し、日本最古の即身仏として現在に至ると説明される。宝物堂には雷獣のミイラも伝わり、死と祈り、民間伝承、寺宝展示が濃く重なる。
highlights: 弘智法印の即身仏を祀る越後の古刹
雷獣のミイラを伝える宝物堂
親鸞上人・松尾芭蕉も参詣した日本最古とされる即身仏
from_kameyama: 車で約420分（東名阪→名神→北陸道）
summary_en: An old temple on the flank of Mt. Yahiko enshrining the sokushinbutsu (self-mummified Buddhist monk) of Kōchi Hōin. The official site states that, after 3,000 days of austerities, Kōchi Hōin entered nyūjō in 1363 and has remained as a sokushinbutsu ever since. The treasure hall also preserves a so-called 'raijū' (thunder beast) mummy — death, prayer, folk lore and temple-treasure display layered densely in a single site.
highlights_en: An old Echigo temple enshrining the sokushinbutsu of Kōchi Hōin
A treasure hall preserving a so-called raijū (thunder beast) mummy
What is regarded as Japan's oldest sokushinbutsu, visited historically by Shinran and Bashō

name: 高鍋大師
name_kana: たかなべだいし
address: 宮崎県児湯郡高鍋町大字持田
summary: 持田古墳群の近くに、故・岩岡保吉氏が私財を投じ還暦過ぎから一人で彫り上げた約750体の神仏混合の石像群が並ぶ。みやざき観光ナビは、盗掘被害にあった古墳に眠る古代人の霊を慰めるために1933年から開山されたと説明する。素朴でデフォルメの強い造形と鎮魂の動機が重なる、全国版向けの強いB級・民俗信仰スポット。
highlights: 約750体の神仏混合の石像群
持田古墳群の盗掘被害への鎮魂を背景にした造形
個人の信仰とアウトサイダーアートが重なる丘
from_kameyama: 車で約760分（新名神→山陽道→九州道→東九州道）
summary_en: Near the Mochida burial mound cluster stands a hill covered in some 750 syncretic stone images, carved single-handedly by the late Iwaoka Yasukichi from his sixties onward. Miyazaki Kankō Navi explains that he began the work in 1933 to console the spirits of the ancients buried in the looted tombs. Naïve, strongly deformed forms meet a motive of memorial — a powerfully Bizarre Japan-grade folk and outsider-art site, fit for the national edition.
highlights_en: Around 750 syncretic Buddhist–Shinto stone images
Founded as a memorial to the looting of the Mochida burial mounds
A hillside where private devotion and outsider art converge

name: 福田海 鼻ぐり塚
name_kana: ふくでんかい はなぐりづか
address: 岡山県岡山市北区吉備津795
summary: 宗教法人福田海本部の境内に、全国から集められた牛の鼻輪を積み上げた供養塚。岡山観光WEBとるるぶは、牛の鼻輪約700万個を積み上げ、馬頭観音を本尊に家畜全般を供養していると説明する。色とりどりの鼻ぐりが巨大な塚を成す光景は異様だが、根底には食と畜類への鎮魂がある。
highlights: 約700万個の牛の鼻輪を積み上げた供養塚
馬頭観音を本尊に家畜全般を供養
食肉・畜産と鎮魂が可視化された大量奉納空間
from_kameyama: 車で約220分（新名神→山陽道）
summary_en: Within the grounds of the religious corporation Fukudenkai stands a memorial mound piled from cattle nose rings gathered from all over Japan. Okayama Kankō Web and Rurubu describe it as a heap of roughly seven million cattle nose rings, dedicated to Batō Kannon as the chief deity in memorial for livestock of every kind. The mound — bright with countless coloured rings — appears outlandish, but at its core lies a serious requiem for meat-producing animals.
highlights_en: A memorial mound piled with around seven million cattle nose rings
Dedicated to Batō Kannon as chief deity, memorialising all livestock
A mass-offering space where meat, livestock husbandry, and requiem are made visible

name: 陰陽石
name_kana: いんようせき
address: 宮崎県小林市東方
summary: 小林市の川沿いに、男石・女石と呼ばれる巨大な自然石が並ぶ奇岩信仰の場。小林市公式によれば男石(陽石)は高さ17.5m、女石(陰石)は周囲5.5mで、霧島火山帯の加久藤火砕流が浸食を受けて形成された自然奇岩とされる。生殖器象徴が明瞭で、子宝・縁結び・夫婦和合の祈願対象として古くから語られる。霧島ジオパークのジオサイト指定。
highlights: 男石(高さ17.5m)・女石(周囲5.5m)と呼ばれる巨大自然石
子宝・縁結び・夫婦和合の祈願対象
霧島ジオパークのジオサイト指定
from_kameyama: 車で約780分（新名神→山陽道→九州道→宮崎道）
summary_en: Along a riverbank in Kobayashi City stand a pair of huge natural rocks known as the Male Stone and the Female Stone — a place of cult around an extraordinary natural formation. According to the City of Kobayashi, the male (yang) stone is about 17.5 m tall and the female (yin) stone about 5.5 m around, formed when the Kakutō pyroclastic flow of the Kirishima volcanic belt was eroded by the river. The phallic and yonic forms are unmistakable, and the rocks have long been worshipped for child-blessing, matchmaking and conjugal harmony. They are also designated as a Kirishima Geopark geosite.
highlights_en: Massive natural rocks known as the Male Stone (17.5 m tall) and the Female Stone (5.5 m around)
An object of prayer for children, matchmaking, and harmony between spouses
Designated as a Kirishima Geopark geosite

name: 軽部神社
name_kana: かるべじんじゃ
address: 岡山県総社市清音軽部
summary: 延宝6年(1678年)建立とされる神社で、境内にあった『垂乳根の桜』にちなみ乳神様として信仰を集めた。総社市公式は、安産や母乳の出を願うため、乳房を型取った手作りの絵馬が数多く奉納されていると説明する。身体信仰と大量奉納が視覚的に残る、岡山の民俗信仰スポット。
highlights: 乳神様として信仰される神社
乳房を型取った手作り絵馬が多数奉納
安産・母乳・乳の病に関わる身体信仰
from_kameyama: 車で約210分（新名神→山陽道）
summary_en: A shrine said to have been founded in 1678, which gathered devotion as 'the breast deity' from a 'Tarachine cherry tree' once standing in its precincts. The City of Sōja explains that worshippers praying for safe birth and for breast milk dedicate many hand-made ema in the shape of breasts. A folk-belief site where bodily devotion and mass votive offerings remain vividly visible.
highlights_en: A shrine venerated as 'the breast deity'
Many hand-made ema shaped like breasts dedicated as offerings
Bodily devotion tied to safe birth, breast milk, and breast ailments

name: 淡嶋神社
name_kana: あわしまじんじゃ
address: 和歌山県和歌山市加太118
fee: 無料、宝物殿は300円(要予約)
summary: 和歌山市加太に鎮座し、全国の淡島神社・粟島神社の総本社とされる神社。少彦名命を祭神とし、医薬・安産・女性の病気回復の信仰と結びつく。境内には全国から納められた2万体以上の人形が並び、3月3日には人形を船に乗せ海に流す『雛流し』神事が行われる。心霊的に煽られやすい場所だが、Bizarre Japanでは人形供養と女性信仰の民俗として扱う。
highlights: 境内を埋める2万体以上の奉納人形
全国淡島神社・粟島神社の総本社
3月3日『雛流し』神事と2月8日『針供養』
from_kameyama: 車で約150分（名阪国道→京奈和道→阪和道）
summary_en: A shrine in Kada, Wakayama City, known nationwide for memorial rites for dolls. Within its precincts stand great numbers of dolls offered from all over Japan, in connection with prayers for recovery from women's illnesses and for safe birth. Although the site is easily framed in 'haunted' terms, on Bizarre Japan we treat it strictly as a folk-religion site of doll memorial and women's devotion.
highlights_en: Precincts filled with great numbers of offered dolls
A Kada shrine famed for ningyō-kuyō (doll memorial)
Tied to belief in recovery from women's illnesses and safe birth

name: 飯野高宮神山神社
name_kana: いいのたかみやこうやまじんじゃ
address: 三重県松阪市山添町4
summary: 松阪市山添町に鎮座する式内社とされる神社。境内・参道をJR紀勢本線が物理的に横断する構造が特異で、神域と近代鉄道が同じ空間で交差する珍しい事例として知られる。線路横断部は踏切扱いで、参拝の際は安全に配慮する必要がある。神社そのものの祭祀は通常の式内社として継承されている。
highlights: 境内・参道をJR紀勢本線が横切る稀な構造
式内社とされる古社で神域に鉄道が交差
踏切を渡って参拝する形になる動線
from_kameyama: 車で約1時間（伊勢道→国道166号方面）
summary_en: A shrine in Yamazoe-cho, Matsusaka, said to be a shikinaisha (listed in the 10th-century Engishiki). Its distinguishing feature is that the JR Kisei Main Line physically crosses the shrine precincts and approach path, creating an unusual case in which a sacred site and a modern railway share the same ground. Visitors cross at a level crossing on the way to worship; ritual life at the shrine itself continues in the ordinary manner of a shikinaisha.
highlights_en: A rare layout in which the JR Kisei Main Line crosses through the precincts and approach
A shikinaisha-class old shrine whose sacred area intersects an active rail line
Worshippers must cross a railway level crossing to reach the shrine

name: 珍布峠と礫石
name_kana: めずらしとうげ と つぶていし
address: 三重県松阪市飯高町赤桶
hours: 通行自由（旧街道ウォーキング推奨時間帯）
summary: 松阪市飯高町赤桶にある旧街道の切り通し峠と、それに付随する伝承石「礫石」。観光三重は、天照大神と天児屋根命がこの地で出会い「おお、めずらしや」と言ったことから珍布峠と呼ばれると説明し、さらに天照大神が川に投げ入れて国境を決めたと伝わる礫石が見える地点として紹介している。地名民俗と国分け伝説が一体で残る場所。
highlights: 「めずらし峠」という地名そのものに残る神話的由来
天照大神と天児屋根命の邂逅伝説
国分け伝説に登場する礫石が川中に残る
from_kameyama: 車で約1時間20分（伊勢道→国道166号方面）
summary_en: An old-road cut-through pass in Akaoke, Iitaka-cho, Matsusaka, paired with the legendary boulder known as Tsubute-ishi. Tradition of the encounter between Amaterasu and Ame-no-Koyane
Tsubute-ishi, the boulder of the land-dividing legend, visible in the river

Interior lighting that makes the cave straightforward to visit
A roughly 30-minute walk from JR Aso Station into the hills

name_en: Kujira no Kuyo-to Whale Memorial Tower
summary_en: An Edo-period memorial stone in Nigishima-cho, Kumano. Kanko Mie records that it was erected in Kanbun 11 (1671) and that its face is inscribed 'Memorial Tower for Thirty-three Whales.' In Kumano fishing folklore, taking thirty-three of a major fish (yellowtail, tuna, etc.) was celebrated as 'Man-no-Iwai' (Celebration of Ten Thousand), and this tower is said to have been raised in connection with that practice. The site sits at the intersection of animal memorial tradition and the religious life of a fishing community.
highlights_en: An Edo-period stele inscribed 'Memorial Tower for Thirty-three Whales' (1671)
Tied to the 'Man-no-Iwai' custom of marking every 33 yellowtail or tuna caught
A folk-religion stone where animal memorial and maritime livelihood meet

name_en: Kuki Yoshitaka Head Mound and Body Mound
summary_en: Two separate burial sites on Tōshi-jima island, where the head and body of the Sengoku-era Kuki navy commander Kuki Yoshitaka were interred apart. Kanko Mie records that, per his will, his head was buried at the summit of Mt. Tsukijo with a view over Toba Castle; Ise-Shima Kanko Navi explains that the body mound stands in the town center of Wagu Fishing Port, near the former Tōsen-an temple site and the 'Chiarai-ike' (blood-washing pond). The fact that the head and body mounds are physically separated on the island makes this site readable as a folk-religion record of a divided-body burial tradition, rather than as an ordinary samurai gravesite.
highlights_en: Head Mound at the summit of Mt. Tsukijo; Body Mound in Wagu Port village
Head burial chosen to overlook Toba Castle, per Kuki Yoshitaka's will
Former Tōsen-an temple site and 'Chiarai-ike' pond remain near the body mound

name_en: Mishiodono Shrine and Sacred Salt Route

Read together with the Mishio-michi (Sacred Salt Route) along which brine from the Mishio-hama salt fields is carried to the shrine, the site forms an unusual production-ritual complex on the periphery of Jingū.

A two-stage process: reduction at the Mishio-yakisho and firing at the Mishio-dono
The 'Mishio-michi' route along which brine is carried from the salt fields

summary_en: A small, ancient shrine deep in the mountains beyond the Akakura settlement in Ikuo-cho, Kumano City. The Kumano City Tourism Association explains that the shrine takes a massive boulder as its sacred body, reflecting an iwakura (sacred-rock) tradition rooted in the area before pilgrims began visiting the Kumano Sanzan, and notes the striking sight of trees growing from the top of the rock. An ancient nature-worship site said to predate the Kumano Sanzan pilgrimage tradition
Distinctive landscape of trees growing on top of the sacred boulder

summary_en: A small shrine on Mt. Hōrai (also called Maruyama) in Hadasu-cho, Kumano City, dedicated to Xu Fu (Jofuku), a figure said to have been sent by China's Qin Shi Huang in search of an elixir of immortality and to have settled in this area. The Xu Fu story is a local tradition rather than confirmed history, but the shrine is notable as a small site that enshrines a continental immigrant as a deity, set within the village landscape of the Iseji route of the Kumano Kodō.

Located on Mt. Hōrai (Maruyama), near the Iseji route of the Kumano Kodō and the Hadasu post-village

summary_en: An ancient Tendai-Shinsei sect temple in Asada-cho, Matsusaka. The principal Jizo Bosatsu statue is a National Important Cultural Property. The temple is known for the 'kake-koromo' (hanging garment) tradition: bereaved families hang the beloved clothes of the deceased in the main hall, on the storehouse, and from the trees in the grounds, praying for the dead to find their way to enlightenment. The result is a striking sight of countless kimono, Western clothes, and obi sashes hanging throughout the precincts. Offered garments are burned each year on November 24 in the 'Domyo Kuyo' memorial rite. The main hall (built 1652, hip-and-gable roof with tile) is a Mie Prefectural Cultural Property, and fusuma paintings by Soga Shohaku are kept here. This entry treats the site through the folkloric lens of memorialization of the dead — not as the supernatural.

summary_en: A roughly 55-meter-long electric-lit giant dragon dance offered at the Gion festival of Seno Shrine in Kurima-Machiyacho, Tsu City. Local volunteers known as the 'Machiya Hyakuninshu' (literally 'Hundred Townspeople') carry the dragon along the old Ise highway and out to National Route 23 in the evening. A modern folk event that doubles as a rain-prayer and community-bonding rite, it now faces existential challenges as the preservation group ages and successors become scarce; crowdfunding campaigns have been launched to sustain it. This entry frames the dragon as both a powerful nighttime spectacle and a story of community succession.

name_en: Ueno Tenjin Festival Danjiri & Demon Procession (Sugawara Shrine)
summary_en: The autumn festival of Sugawara Shrine (Ueno Tenjin) in Iga City. Over one hundred performers wear Noh and Kyogen masks in a 'demon procession' that winds through the former castle town alongside nine danjiri floats. Centered on the fourth Sunday of October across three days, the danjiri event is designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan and was inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2016. Coordinates are at Sugawara Shrine, about a 5-minute walk from Iga-Ueno Station.

name_en: Miyamado Inari Shrine (Thousand Foxes & Petrochemical Skyline)
summary_en: A shrine in Miyamadocho, Yokkaichi City. The auxiliary 'Miyamado Kaiun Inari Shrine' on the grounds is actually larger than the main hall; its precincts are packed with hundreds of fox statues donated from across Japan, producing an overwhelming visual density. Behind the shrine rise the chimneys of the Yokkaichi petrochemical complex, and in a single frame, an old fox-cult shrine and postwar heavy industry coexist — a peculiarly Mie 'otherworldly' landscape. Excellent photography access right in front of Kintetsu Miyamado Station. Locally nicknamed 'Miyamado-san.'
highlights_en: Roughly a thousand donated fox statues packed across the grounds

summary_en: A ritual held every February 3rd (Setsubun) at Miyamado Shrine (the Miyamado Kaiun Inari Shrine on its grounds) in Yokkaichi City. A pure-white bride and an attendant procession in fox masks walk from the surrounding streets into the shrine grounds, reenacting the wedding of the trickster fox. summary_en: A lion dance ritual passed down in Yamagami, Tamaki Town in Watarai District. In addition to the lion dance, a tengu performer appears, and spectators hurl water-soaked pinecones at the tengu to drive away disease and evil — a rare participatory folk performance. The form recalls the bean-throwing of Setsubun and is considered a survival of older purification rites. Held at Yamagami Shrine around the small new year (early January) each year by the local preservation society. Coordinates are a representative value for the center of Yamagami-cho.

summary_en: A maritime safety ritual at Nakiri Shrine in Nakiri, Daioh-cho, Shima City. Children drag a giant straw sandal the size of a tatami mat down to the harbor, where it is set adrift. Local tradition links the rite to a legend in which a one-eyed sea monster called 'Dandara-Hoshi,' said to have appeared off Cape Daioh, was driven off by tricking it with an enormous sandal that suggested an even larger person was nearby. Designated an Intangible Folk Cultural Property by Shima City and emblematic of the coastal faith of the fishing town. Coordinates are a representative value for the center of Nakiri-cho.

summary_en: An ancient shrine in Kawachi, Minami-Ise Town in Watarai District. Perched atop a roughly 70-meter hill, the main hall is reached by a flight of over 360 stone steps that begin beside the sacred 'Tree of Resurrection' (a Bakuchi tree). On the rocky slope behind the main hall, a massive rock outcrop known as 'Sarushinseki' (Monkey God Stone) bears a profile resembling a monkey's face, said in local tradition to be the deity Sarutahiko transformed into stone to guard the land. The iwakura (sacred rock) group behind the main hall is an ancient ritual site that has yielded many artifacts and is designated a cultural property as a shrine archaeological site. The picture-tablet hall displays paintings inspired by the Hyakunin Isshu poems and the Tale of the Heavenly Rock Cave.
highlights_en: 'Sarushinseki' (Monkey God Stone): a massive iwakura associated with Sarutahiko

summary_en: A roughly 300-year-old fire ritual held at Obuke Shrine in Asahi Town, Mie District. On the night of August 14 every year, parishioners strike each other with burning straw bundles, eventually setting alight a 5- to 6-meter great torch. Designated a Mie Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property. The combination of sparks, straw bundles, and the bodily clash of strikers in the dark is overwhelming — an example where, in the framework of this Space, the 'fusion of unusual form and ritual function' reaches its peak. Night-time fire shooting demands care for equipment and safety. About a 10-minute walk from JR Asahi Station; parking available.
